editorial:
D.O.A. is a 1950 film noir directed by Rudolph Maté and starring Edmond O'Brien and Pamela Britton. Harry Popkin Productions and Cardinal Pictures made it. Clarence Greene and Russell Rouse wrote the screenplay, and Dimitri Tiomkin is credited with the score. A poisoned man walks into a police station to report his own murder, and he spends the rest of the film finding out who did it. That opening tracking shot is among the most recognisable in noir. The Library of Congress chose the film for the National Film Registry in 2004. Creators reuse it often for clips, remixes and noir-themed edits.

The Public Domain Review says the film is in the public domain in the US because its copyright was not renewed. That is a secondary claim. This dossier could not check the renewal records themselves, so the print stays undetermined until someone searches the Catalog of Copyright Entries and the Copyright Office catalog. The rights trap is the layers beyond the picture. The Tiomkin score and the underlying screenplay may carry their own registrations. Any restored or re-scored release may also add protected material. Check each of those before commercial reuse.
faq: Secondary sources say its copyright lapsed through a missed renewal. This dossier could not confirm that in the primary renewal records, so search the Stanford renewal database and the Copyright Office catalog yourself before relying on it. The score, the story and any modern restoration should be checked separately.
Where can I watch or download a copy?

The Internet Archive has an item at archive.org/details/DOA1950, and its metadata confirms the title and year. The quality of that copy was not verified. A restored release may include added material, such as new titles or a new score, that is protected separately.
